# Requirement History

## What It Is

Requirement History keeps a permanent, readable record of *why* each capability in your system is the way it is. Specs describe what a system must do, but the reasoning — the conversations, design decisions, and approved plans that shaped those specs — usually disappears into chat sessions and people's memories. This feature captures that reasoning and links it directly to the capabilities it influenced, so future contributors, reviewers, and automated agents can understand the intent behind a requirement before changing or removing it.

> **Note:** This feature is planned and not yet fully built. The underlying file structure is already in place, but the commands, hooks, and reporting described below are still in development.

---

## What You Can Do With It

### Record a decision by hand

When you finish a design discussion and want to preserve the outcome, run:

```
specguard history add --decision "Docs responses are not streamed" --affects documentation-api
```

This creates a dated, readable entry under `specs/history/` and links it back to the capability you named. You can also record a prompt or an approved plan instead of a decision.

### Let hooks capture sessions automatically

If you opt your repository in with `specguard init --history-hooks`, SpecGuard will watch your Claude Code sessions. When you approve a plan, SpecGuard automatically saves the prompts from that session and the approved plan as a single history entry. Sessions that never reach an approved plan are not recorded. You can run this setup command again safely — it will not overwrite your existing hooks unless you explicitly ask it to.

### Read the history of a capability

```
specguard history log --capability security-and-remediation
```

This prints a timeline of every entry linked to that capability, newest first, showing the date, kind of entry, title, and which capabilities it affected. Add `--json` to get the same output in a machine-readable format.

### Find unexplained changes

```
specguard check
```

This includes a report of any capability whose source files changed since its last history entry or spec edit, with no recorded reason. By default this is advisory; your project can opt in to treating it as a build failure.

### Let agents read history before editing

Coding agents can read the history entries linked from a capability spec before making changes. This prevents them from undoing a decision that was made deliberately.

---

## What a History Entry Contains

Each entry is a readable file with:

- A unique identifier and date
- The kind of record it is: a **prompt**, an **approved plan**, a **decision**, or a combination such as **prompt+plan**
- Who created it and how (manually or from a Claude Code session)
- Which capabilities it affects
- The verbatim text of the prompt, plan, or decision

History entries are not specs. They do not appear in the spec graph, and changing only the history links on a spec does not invalidate any existing proofs or approvals.

---

## Secrets and Privacy

Prompts often contain sensitive information. SpecGuard applies redaction twice — once when a prompt is first captured and again when an entry is committed — so keys, tokens, and personal data are replaced with placeholders before anything is saved to your repository. Unprocessed prompt data is held in a local file that is never committed. History recording is always opt-in; no prompts are captured unless you have explicitly enabled the hooks.

If a sensitive value does slip through redaction, you should edit the committed file to remove it and rotate the affected secret.

---

## What It Does Not Do

- It does not capture full chat transcripts or tool output — only prompts, approved plans, and explicit decisions.
- It does not replace your git history, issue tracker, or pull request discussions.
- It does not automatically rewrite or delete past entries.
- In this first version it only integrates with Claude Code; other AI coding tools are not supported.
